opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we've thought about a lot, because the early team is what gets you to product-market fit, and it's easy to lose what made them effective as you scale.

A few things have mattered most. First, keep the core team focused on a small number of really important problems. As a company grows there are a hundred things pulling at people, like customer escalations, internal process, and new initiatives. If your strongest engineers and researchers get spread across all of it, they stop moving the needle. So you have to deliberately protect their time and say, "this group owns this hard problem, and everything else gets handled somewhere else."

Second, ownership. Small teams work because everyone knows what they own and can make decisions quickly. As you grow, the natural tendency is to add layers and coordination, and suddenly every decision needs five people in a room. We try to structure things so teams stay relatively small, have clear ownership of a product area or a technical component, and can ship without waiting on everyone else. Good interfaces between teams matter almost as much as good interfaces in software.

Third, hiring and onboarding. The core team's culture gets diluted quickly if you hire fast without thinking about it. Having senior people involved in hiring, and pairing new folks with experienced people early on, helps a lot. A lot of how you work, like how you write design docs, how you think about reliability, and how you talk to customers, is tacit knowledge, and it gets transferred by working together, not by reading a wiki.

And finally, staying close to users. In the early days everybody talks to customers. As you grow, that tends to get pushed to sales and support, and the engineering team loses that direct signal. We try hard to keep engineers and researchers hearing directly from users, because that's what keeps the work grounded and keeps people motivated. It's much easier to stay effective when you can see the impact of what you're building.

So there's no silver bullet. It's mostly about being intentional: protect focus, keep ownership clear, be careful about how you grow, and don't let the team drift away from the people actually using the product.

r001.rationale: The response mentions senior people helping with hiring and onboarding and transferring tacit knowledge by working together, but does not say company leaders spend substantial time working hands-on with the team.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because I've been through it a couple of times now, first with Spark and the Databricks founding team, and then watching it play out again as the company got much bigger. And honestly I don't think I had a good theory of it at the start. We just sort of stumbled into things that worked.

The first thing I'd say is that the thing that makes a small team effective is usually that everyone has a lot of context. In the early days of Spark, everyone on the team basically knew the whole codebase, they knew what users were complaining about, they knew why we made certain design decisions. So when a problem came up, you didn't need a meeting, you just fixed it. And as you grow, the natural failure mode is that context gets fragmented. People start working on narrower pieces, and then decisions that used to take an afternoon take three weeks because you have to route them through five people who each have a part of the picture.

So a lot of what I try to do is preserve context rather than preserve the specific people or the specific org structure. That means being pretty deliberate about writing things down, which engineers hate, but it matters. It means keeping the core technical people close to actual users for as long as possible, even when it would be more "efficient" to put layers in between. Some of the best product decisions we made came from engineers who had just gotten off a call with a customer and were kind of annoyed about something.

The second thing is that you have to let the core team's role change. Early on, those people are writing most of the code. Later, their highest leverage is setting direction and taste, and reviewing the hard stuff, and making the calls that nobody else has the confidence to make. If you don't make that shift explicitly, you end up with your most experienced people either burning out trying to do everything or getting frustrated because they feel like they're not contributing the way they used to. We definitely had moments like that.

And then the last thing, which is maybe less obvious, is that the core team has to stay a little bit uncomfortable. The risk when a company succeeds is that the early people get very good at defending what already exists, because they built it. We tried to counter that by having some of the original folks go start new things inside the company, like the work on the lakehouse ideas or more recently the LLM and agents efforts. That keeps them in the mode of being builders rather than just custodians, and it also sets a cultural signal that the interesting work isn't all behind us.

I'd say we got maybe two out of three of those right at any given time, which is probably about what you can hope for.

r001.rationale: The response says core team members write code early on and later shift toward direction-setting and reviewing hard work, but it does not identify company leaders spending substantial time working hands-on with the team.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to keep the core team focused on a small number of problems where working closely together really matters. As the company grows, there are more requests, more meetings, and more things you could be doing. If every decision has to come back to that team, it becomes a bottleneck.

So you need to give other teams clear ownership and enough context to make decisions independently. And for the core team, you want to preserve time to actually build things and stay close to users. Otherwise, you can end up spending all your time coordinating and lose the feedback that made the team effective in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says the core team should preserve time to build and work closely together, but it does not identify company leaders spending substantial time working hands-on with the team.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to keep the core team focused on a small number of problems where working closely together really matters. As the company grows, there are more requests, more meetings, and more people who need context. If every decision still has to go through that original group, they become a bottleneck.

So you need to build teams that can own things independently, with clear goals and enough context to make good decisions. And then protect time for the core team to actually build and experiment. You want their impact to grow through the systems they create and the people they enable, rather than through the number of decisions they personally approve.

r001.rationale: The response says the core team should build and experiment and work closely together, but it does not identify company leaders spending substantial time working hands-on with the team.
